result:
The proposed answer is very likely wrong. The solution never derives its formula; it asserts a "known theorem" and an unjustified construction.

A check at r = 3 shows the leading term cannot be (r−2)n for every s > r−2.

- Suppose a triangle-saturated graph has a vertex ℓ of degree 1, with neighbor v. Every vertex w not adjacent to ℓ needs a common neighbor with ℓ, so w must be adjacent to v. Hence v is adjacent to all other vertices.
- The neighborhood of v is triangle-free-forced to be independent, so G − v has no edges. The matching number is then 1.
- So for matching number at least 2, a large triangle-saturated graph has no degree-1 vertices, which forces roughly 2n edges, not n−1+const. For example, K_{2,n−2} has matching number 2.

The same effect appears for general r. Once the matching number exceeds r−2, the base extremal graph K_{r−2} ∨ (independent set) is no longer allowed. A different structure is needed, and it costs more than a linear-in-s correction to (r−2)n − C(r−1,2).

Adding a matching of size s−r+2 inside the independent set also does not work as claimed. Those edges would break saturation, since non-edges between the new matched vertices and the rest would not all create K_r.

The proposed formula is therefore not justified and almost certainly incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
